opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the key idea is that with a reconfigurable dataflow architecture, you're not executing the model one kernel at a time the way you would on a GPU. On a GPU, the typical pattern is that you launch a kernel for, say, the QKV projection, it reads its inputs from HBM, computes, writes the results back to HBM, and then the next kernel, attention, reads them back in. Every one of those intermediate tensors makes a round trip across the memory boundary, and for decode, where you're processing one token or a small batch at a time, you end up completely memory-bandwidth bound. You're just shuffling activations back and forth.

What we do with the RDU is take the dataflow graph of the decoder, the whole transformer block or even multiple blocks, and map it spatially onto the chip. The RDU has a grid of pattern compute units, which do the math, and pattern memory units, which are distributed on-chip SRAM, all connected by a programmable on-chip network. So the compiler lays out the operators in space: the layer norm, the projections, the attention computation, the softmax, the MLP, and the outputs of one stage stream directly into the next stage through the on-chip interconnect and get staged in those distributed memories. We pipeline it so that different stages are working on different pieces of data at the same time.

The result is that the intermediate activations, the stuff internal to the decoder, never leave the chip. They live in SRAM and flow between units. The only things you go out to HBM for are the things that fundamentally have to live there: the weights and the KV cache. And we try to make even those accesses efficient by streaming the weights in and overlapping that with compute.

We call this operator fusion, but it's fusion at a much more aggressive scale than you can do on a GPU, where you're limited by what fits in a single kernel and in shared memory. Because the hardware is reconfigurable, the compiler can essentially fuse an entire decoder into one big streaming dataflow pipeline.

And then there's a third level of memory below HBM, a large DDR tier, which lets us hold many models or very large models and swap them into HBM quickly. But for the question of keeping internal decoder data off the HBM boundary, it really comes down to spatial mapping plus streaming dataflow plus lots of distributed on-chip memory. That's what lets us get much higher tokens per second on decode, because you're spending your HBM bandwidth only on the data that really needs it.

r001.rationale: The response says the decoder graph is mapped spatially onto an RDU chip, but it does not describe mapping it across multiple RDUs; it refers to “the RDU” in the singular.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks, Sam, it's great to be back. So the core idea is really about where the data lives during a decode step. If you look at a conventional GPU running a decoder, every operator in the transformer block is essentially its own kernel. You load weights and activations from HBM, you do a matmul or a layer norm or a softmax, you write the result back to HBM, and then the next kernel picks it up again. For a decode step, where you're generating one token at a time with batch sizes that aren't enormous, you're memory-bandwidth bound, and all of that intermediate traffic in and out of HBM is wasted bandwidth that's eating into your token latency.

A reconfigurable dataflow unit flips that model. Instead of a sequence of kernels, you take the whole decoder layer, or a large chunk of it, and you spatially map it onto the chip. The compute units get configured to do the attention projections, the softmax, the output projection, the feedforward layers, and so on, and the on-chip memory units get configured as the buffers between them. Then you literally wire the stages together through the on-chip interconnect. So the output of one operation streams directly into the input of the next, through the on-chip SRAM, without ever leaving the die. The HBM boundary only gets crossed for the things that genuinely have to come from off-chip, which in decode is mostly streaming the weights and the KV cache through once.

The key enabler is that the chip has a lot of distributed SRAM, hundreds of megabytes, and it's not a cache. It's explicitly managed by the compiler. So the compiler looks at the dataflow graph of the model, figures out which tensors are intermediates that only exist between two operators, and allocates those to on-chip memory. It also does the pipelining and tiling so that you can overlap the weight streaming from HBM with the compute that's already happening on-chip. What that buys you is that your effective bandwidth is the on-chip bandwidth, which is an order of magnitude or more higher than HBM, and you're using the HBM bandwidth almost entirely for weights rather than for shuffling activations around.

The other thing I'd point out is that this is where the "reconfigurable" part really matters. Different models and different phases, prefill versus decode, have different shapes, and the mapping of operators to compute and memory units gets regenerated by the compiler for each one. You're not stuck with a fixed pipeline baked into silicon. And when the model is bigger than one chip, the same dataflow idea extends across the fabric between chips, so you're doing the same kind of streaming rather than going back through host memory. So in short, it's not a trick, it's just a consequence of treating the model as a dataflow graph and having enough on-chip memory and interconnect that the graph's internal edges never have to touch HBM.

r001.rationale: The response describes spatially mapping a decoder layer or chunk onto a chip, but does not say the decoder is mapped across multiple RDUs.

astra-6.text:
The idea is to map the computation as a pipeline of operations, rather than execute each operation as a separate kernel. With separate kernels, you often write an intermediate result out to HBM and then read it back for the next operation. That movement is expensive.

With reconfigurable dataflow units, we configure both the computation and the paths between operations. So an intermediate result can flow directly to the next operation, or stay in on-chip memory until it’s needed. Within a decoder block, that lets us fuse sequences of operations and avoid repeatedly sending those intermediate activations across the HBM interface.

That doesn’t mean everything in the LLM fits on chip. You still need to bring in weights and access the KV cache when they reside in HBM. The goal is to keep the internal working data on chip for as much of the computation as possible, so you spend bandwidth on necessary transfers rather than on materializing every intermediate result.

r001.rationale: The response describes configuring dataflow paths and fusing operations within a decoder block, but does not say that a single LLM decoder is spatially mapped across multiple RDUs.

sol-6.1.text:
The key is to map the computation so that intermediate results stay on the chip. In a reconfigurable dataflow architecture, you configure both the compute units and the connections between them. The output of one operation can flow directly into the next, with on-chip memory holding data where you need buffering or reuse.

For a decoder, that means fusing operations so you don’t write every intermediate activation out to HBM and then read it back for the next operation. You bring in the weights and the data you need, perform as much of the computation as possible on chip, and write back what you actually need to retain.

That doesn’t mean the entire model or KV cache fits on chip. You still have capacity constraints. But you can organize the computation into tiles and stream those tiles through the configured dataflow, substantially reducing the traffic across that HBM boundary.

r001.rationale: The response discusses configuring compute units and connections to keep decoder intermediates on chip, but it does not clearly say that a single LLM decoder is spatially mapped across multiple RDUs.
